newsitem.title: CANADA: Nortel CEO mum on whether he will stay at helm.
newsitem.headline: Nortel CEO mum on whether he will stay at helm.

text.p: (All figures in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted)
By Sarah Edmonds
Jean Monty, credited with turning around Canada's flagship high-technology company, neatly sidesteps the question the market is asking -- whether he will stay at the helm of Northern Telecom Ltd.
"My sense is that I will continue to be associated with Northern and with (the BCE family of) companies for years to come," Monty, 49, said in an interview this week with Reuters.
"I can't answer (whether this association will be as chief executive). That I just can't answer until we have had that discussion with the board."

Monty's future at Nortel is a hot topic of concern among analysts and investors, who give him high marks for transforming the once-troubled telecommunications equipment maker, which is 51.2 percent-owned by Canadian telecommunications firm BCE Inc..
His four-year tenure has seen a huge restructuring and software revamp, with Nortel shares now trading at lofty heights.
Monty's conservative management style contrasts with that of his mercurial predecessor Paul Stern.

"The management team which was shaken (up) four-and-a-half years ago has changed significantly. It has matured," said Monty, speaking from the company's new head office in Brampton, Ontario, a Toronto suburb.
He declined to comment on whether he has been approached by other firms.
"Everybody, whether you have a contract or not, that has had some success, is bound to be approached by all sorts of people for all sorts of positions, CEO or whatever," he said.

"I want to find a proposition which will be attractive to all concerned in driving that potential forward. I think that in time (management) will be ready to go without me sitting at the helm," Monty added.
He quipped that the chief executive's chair at Nortel was desirable now the company had recovered its luster.
"It's a great job now. But nobody wanted the job four or five years ago," Monty said.
In the second quarter of 1993, just after Monty succeeded Stern, Nortel stunned investors with a huge restructuring charge and a $1.03 billion loss.
The company lost $884 million for full-year 1993.
In contrast, Nortel's earnings rose 32 percent in 1996 to $623 million or $2.40 a share, levels unseen since the days before the restructuring.
Revenue rose 20 percent last year to $12.85 billion from $10.7 billion the year before.
Monty said sales should jump between 15 and 20 percent in 1997, with earnings growing outstripping that.
Many analysts have buy or strong buy ratings on Nortel with fairly aggressive 12-month price targets.
The stock is trading high enough for many analysts to speculate about a stock split, especially given a similar move last month by parent BCE.
But Monty ruled that out.
Nortel shares were down C$1 to C$95.50 in Toronto Stock Exchange trading on Tuesday and fell by 75 cents to $70.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
